summary.name: "It's dead, Jim": How we write an incident postmortem
summary.one_liner: A Hosted Graphite blog article explaining what an incident postmortem is, why it matters, who should write it, and how to prepare one in a blameless, learning-focused way.
use_cases: Writing a postmortem after a production outage
Deciding whether an incident deserves a written review
Running a blameless incident review with a team
Building a timeline and questions for incident analysis
Learning SRE incident culture and practices
summary.what_it_does: The article defines a postmortem as the written record of an incident, covering its impact, mitigation actions, and lessons learned with follow-up tasks. It explains why postmortems matter, such as documenting incidents, driving infrastructure improvements, and communicating with users. It advises on when to write one, noting that the on-call engineer usually decides and that publishing within about a week is ideal. It also describes a blameless approach and suggests first steps: building a timeline and asking probing questions about detection, impact, luck, and contributing factors.
notable: Emphasizes blameless postmortems focused on systemic contributing factors rather than individuals
Recommends writing postmortems even for near-incidents and common incidents, treating recurring issues as aggregate signals
Lists required reading including John Allspaw and Richard Cook works on complex systems failure
Part of a series on Hosted Graphite's SRE process
caveats: This is an opinion/process article, not a software tool; it names no template in this excerpt and the template is promised in a later part
Pricing and product details are not applicable
